module callbacks
  /// Task-safe application dependencies captured by request handlers.
  ///
  /// The repository is a host resource handle. Its Host API schema declares
  /// `database.Connection` task-safe, which is what lets this whole struct be
  /// captured by a closure that crosses into a task.
  export struct App
    field repository: database.Connection
    field metrics: Shared<Metrics>
  /// A booking this service stored.
  export struct Booking
    field id: String
  /// Something a request did that subscribers may care about.
  export enum Event
    case BookingCreated(String)
  /// Immutable event subscriptions shared by request tasks.
  export struct EventBus
    field subscribers: Map<String, Array<EventHandler>>
  /// A callback stored by the event bus.
  export type EventHandler = async fn(event: Event) -> Result<Unit, Error>
  /// A callback stored by the router and invoked for each request.
  export type Handler = async fn(request: http.Request) -> Result<http.Response, Error>
  /// Mutable counters shared across request tasks.
  export struct Metrics
    field requests: Int
    field failures: Int
  /// Immutable routes shared by all request tasks.
  export struct Router
    field routes: Array<http.Route>
  /// Runs a server with immutable routes and structured background work.
  export async fn main() -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires clock, console, database, http
    capability-open

module codegen
  /// Builds the `httpstatus.StatusCode` module from `files/status_codes.txt`,
  /// which pairs each numeric code with a `PascalCase` case name as
  /// alternating whitespace-separated tokens: `200 Ok 404 NotFound ...`. One
  /// data file driving both the enum's cases and its `code()` accessor is what
  /// keeps them from drifting apart the way two hand-written lists would.
  export fn statusCodes() -> Result<String, Error>
    requires files

module config
  /// Validated application configuration.
  export struct Config
    field port: Int
    field logLevel: LogLevel
  /// Configuration validation failures.
  export enum ConfigError
    case InvalidPort(String)
    case InvalidLogLevel(String)
  /// Supported logging levels.
  export enum LogLevel
    case Debug
    case Info
    case Warn
    case Error
  /// Loads configuration from the host environment.
  export fn loadConfig() -> Result<Config, ConfigError>
    requires env

module covecheck
  /// One endpoint a run asks about, and what its answer has to look like.
  ///
  /// Every condition is optional except the two that say which endpoint this
  /// is. A check that writes none of them still says something -- that the
  /// endpoint answers at all -- and that is the check most manifests start
  /// with.
  export struct Check
    field name: String
    field url: String
    field expect: Option<String>
    field reject: Option<String>
    field maxLength: Option<Int>
  /// Which of the two reports a run writes.
  export enum Format
    case Text
    case Json
    /// The word this format is asked for by.
    export fn name(self) -> String
  /// Every check of one run, in the order the manifest wrote them.
  ///
  /// The order is part of the manifest rather than an accident of it: it is
  /// what the report comes back in, whatever order the checks finish in.
  export struct Manifest
    field checks: Array<Check>
  /// What a run made of one check.
  ///
  /// The two ways of failing are kept apart because they are different news. A
  /// `Failed` endpoint answered and said the wrong thing, which is a fact about
  /// the service; an `Unchecked` one produced no body to look at, so this run
  /// learned nothing about it and reports that rather than a verdict it did not
  /// reach.
  ///
  /// `Unchecked` covers two things at once because the `http` host gives a
  /// client one answer for both: `fetch` produces an `Err` for a connection it
  /// could not make and an `Err` for a status outside 200-299, and which it was
  /// survives only in the prose of the message. That is also why no check here
  /// names an expected status. Issue #145 is that gap.
  export enum Outcome
    case Passed(Int)
    case Failed(String)
    case Unchecked(String)
    case Skipped
    /// What a report says beside the label.
    export fn detail(self) -> String
    /// The word a report puts in its first column.
    export fn label(self) -> String
    /// Whether this is an outcome the run may end successfully on.
    ///
    /// A skipped check is not one. The run stopped because enough had already
    /// gone wrong, and reporting the checks it never tried as fine would say
    /// the opposite of what happened.
    export fn ok(self) -> Bool
  /// How the run is bounded, beside the checks themselves.
  export struct Plan
    field concurrency: Int
    field stopAfter: Option<Int>
  /// What one run produced.
  export struct Run
    field verdicts: Array<Verdict>
    field tally: Tally
  /// What every check task writes and the run reads between windows.
  ///
  /// `started` is the one thing here that the finished verdicts do not already
  /// say, and it is what tells a report how many checks were never tried. The
  /// counts are kept by the tasks rather than folded out of the array
  /// afterwards because this is the run's one piece of state two tasks reach,
  /// and `lock` is what makes each task's read-modify-write one operation: the
  /// order the increments land in belongs to the scheduler, and the totals do
  /// not depend on it.
  export struct Tally
    field started: Int
    field passed: Int
    field failed: Int
  /// What a run made of one check, and which check it was.
  export struct Verdict
    field name: String
    field url: String
    field outcome: Outcome
  /// The format `name` asks for, or the error that names the two there are.
  export fn formatNamed(name: String) -> Result<Format, Error>
  /// Judges `body` against everything `check` asked of it.
  ///
  /// The conditions are tried in a written order and the first one that breaks
  /// is the whole answer, so two runs over the same body report the same
  /// reason. Reporting every broken condition would be more information and
  /// less of an answer: the length is checked first because a body that is too
  /// large is a fact about the endpoint that the text conditions would then
  /// describe at length.
  export fn judge(check: Check, body: String) -> Outcome
  /// Checks every endpoint one manifest names, and reports what it found.
  ///
  /// The whole run is inside one `clock.timeout`, so a run that will not finish
  /// stops instead of hanging: leaving the bound cancels the window still in
  /// flight, and the checks it held have no verdicts because a cancelled task
  /// has no value to await. That is the honest report of a stopped run. ADR
  /// 0024 makes a stop a bound rather than a point -- a cancelled check stops
  /// within a fixed amount of further work, not at the next instruction -- so
  /// how far each one got is not something this program can say and does not
  /// try to.
  export async fn main(arguments: Array<String>) -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires clock, console, files, http
  /// Reads a manifest out of the text of one file.
  ///
  /// `source` is the file's name and appears in every message, because a
  /// manifest that will not load is the first thing a person meets and the
  /// message is the whole of what they get. There is no line number in it: the
  /// manifest is one JSON document rather than a record per line, so what is
  /// wrong is a path through that document and not a place in the file.
  export fn readManifest(source: String, text: String) -> Result<Manifest, Error>
  /// The report `format` asks for, as the whole text of it.
  ///
  /// Both reports are built and returned rather than printed, so the thing a
  /// test asserts on is the thing a person reads. Neither is written by a task:
  /// a run's tasks share one console and what order their lines would arrive in
  /// is the scheduler's answer, so the report is written once, at the end, by
  /// the one thing that knows the manifest's order.
  export fn report(format: Format, source: String, run: Run) -> String
  /// Runs every check, `plan.concurrency` of them at a time, and answers in
  /// manifest order.
  ///
  /// The order is the whole reason the window is awaited in the order it was
  /// spawned rather than as its tasks finish. Nothing here is faster for
  /// awaiting in order -- a window takes as long as its slowest member either
  /// way -- and what it buys is a report that reads the same twice.
  export async fn runAll(checks: Array<Check>, plan: Plan) -> Run
    requires clock, http
  /// How long a whole run may take.
  ///
  /// The same constant for the same reason, and it bounds the run rather than
  /// the check: a hundred checks that each finish just inside `checkBound` is a
  /// run nobody waited for.
  export fn runBound() -> Duration
  /// How many of a run's checks were never tried.
  ///
  /// The difference between the checks there were and the checks that started,
  /// which is the one number the array of verdicts does not carry on its own.
  export fn skipped(run: Run) -> Int

module cq
  /// Runs one transformation over one file.
  ///
  /// Everything a run needs is decided before a byte is read: which
  /// transformation, which file, which format, and where the output goes. What
  /// happens after that is one loop that never holds more than one record.
  export fn main() -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires console, files, process
    capability-open
  /// Writes a deterministic sample of bookings, for measuring.
  ///
  /// The large input this example's numbers were taken over is not checked in --
  /// a hundred thousand records is fifteen megabytes, and a repository is a bad
  /// place to keep one. It is generated instead, by this, from a seed, so the
  /// file two people measure over is the same file.
  ///
  /// The writer is the same `files.Writer` the transformations write through, so
  /// generating the input is itself a streaming job: this holds one record at a
  /// time exactly as `cq` does.
  export fn sample() -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires console, files, process

module cq.csv
  /// Renders `fields` as one CSV line, without its terminator.
  export fn formatRecord(fields: Array<String>) -> String
  /// Splits one CSV line into its fields.
  ///
  /// The rules are RFC 4180's, with one deliberate exception. A field may be
  /// quoted with `"`, a quoted field may contain commas, and `""` inside a
  /// quoted field is one literal quote. An unquoted field is taken exactly as
  /// written, including any spaces around it: trimming would be this program
  /// deciding that a value the input chose to include was not meant.
  ///
  /// The exception is that a record may not span lines. RFC 4180 lets a quoted
  /// field contain a newline, and the reader upstream of this hands over one
  /// line at a time, so a quoted field that is still open when the line ends is
  /// reported rather than continued. Making it work means the reader and the
  /// splitter having to agree about quoting, which is the format leaking into
  /// the layer whose whole job is not to know about it.
  export fn splitRecord(line: String) -> Result<Array<String>, Detail>

module cq.diag
  /// Where in one line something went wrong, and what.
  ///
  /// A parser knows the column and not the line: it is handed one record at a
  /// time and has no idea which. `locate` is what supplies the rest, at the one
  /// place in the program that is counting.
  export struct Detail
    field column: Int
    field message: String
  /// A detail, once the record it came from is known.
  export struct Diagnostic
    field source: String
    field line: Int
    field column: Int
    field message: String
  /// Reports `diagnostic` the way a compiler reports one, so an editor that
  /// already knows how to jump to `file:line:column` can jump to a bad record.
  export fn describe(diagnostic: Diagnostic) -> String
  /// Places `detail` at line `line` of `source`.
  export fn locate(detail: Detail, source: String, line: Int) -> Diagnostic

module cq.json
  /// A JSON value.
  ///
  /// JSON has one number type, so this does too: an integer that arrived in the
  /// input is a `Number` like any other, and a program that needs an `Int` asks
  /// for one at the point where it knows that is what the field means. Putting
  /// the distinction here instead would be inventing a JSON that the format does
  /// not have.
  export enum Json
    case Null
    case Bool(Bool)
    case Number(Float)
    case Text(String)
    case Items(Array<Json>)
    case Fields(Map<String, Json>)
  /// The field `name` of an object, or `None` for anything else.
  ///
  /// A value that is not an object has no fields rather than an empty set of
  /// them, and both answer `None` here; a caller that needs to tell the two
  /// apart matches on the value itself.
  export fn field(value: Json, name: String) -> Option<Json>
  /// Parses `text` as one complete JSON value.
  ///
  /// The whole of `text` must be that value: trailing content is an error rather
  /// than something the caller is left to notice, because a line of JSON Lines
  /// that has more after the record is not a record with a comment on it.
  export fn parse(text: String) -> Result<Json, Detail>
  /// Renders `value` as JSON on one line, which is what a JSON Lines record is.
  ///
  /// Object fields come out in `Map` order, which is ascending by key, so two
  /// runs over the same input write the same bytes.
  export fn render(value: Json) -> String

module cq.pipeline
  /// What one run did.
  ///
  /// Three counts and nothing else. A run over a hundred thousand records has a
  /// hundred thousand chances to be told something, and a report that kept them
  /// would be the thing this program exists not to do; each diagnostic is
  /// written when it happens and only the tally outlives it.
  ///
  /// `read` counts the records that folded and `skipped` the ones that did not,
  /// so the two together are how many were taken from the input -- which is what
  /// `--limit` bounds.
  export struct Outcome
    field read: Int
    field written: Int
    field skipped: Int
  /// Where a run's output goes.
  ///
  /// The console is not a file this host can open -- `files` is rooted, and a
  /// terminal has no path inside any root -- so writing to one and writing to
  /// the other are two different Host APIs, and this is the one place in the
  /// program that knows which is in use.
  export enum Sink
    case Console
    case File(files.Writer)
  /// Reads every record of `reader`, folds it, and writes what comes back.
  ///
  /// The loop holds one line, one step's rows, and the transformation's own
  /// state. Nothing accumulates that the transformation did not choose to
  /// accumulate, which is what makes the memory a run holds a property of the
  /// program rather than of the file.
  ///
  /// A record that cannot be read stops the run, unless `skipInvalid`, in which
  /// case it is reported and counted and the next record is read. Stopping is
  /// the default because a summary computed from most of the input is a wrong
  /// answer that looks like a right one.
  export fn transform<S>(reader: files.Reader, sink: Sink, source: String, format: Format, columns: Array<String>, initial: S, step: fn(state: S, line: String, number: Int) -> Result<Step<S>, Detail>, finish: fn(state: S) -> Array<Array<Cell>>, skipInvalid: Bool, limit: Option<Int>) -> Result<Outcome, Error>
    requires console
    capability-open

module cq.programs
  /// What the confirmed-bookings transformation carries between records.
  ///
  /// Nothing, and the type says so. This program writes as it reads, one row per
  /// record it keeps, so no part of the input outlives the line it arrived on.
  export struct NoState
    field kept: Int
  /// Which transformation a run performs.
  ///
  /// A program is a case of an enum rather than a file this run loads, because
  /// Cove has no way to load a module at run time: a package is resolved,
  /// checked, and linked before anything executes. So `--program` names one of
  /// the transformations this package declares, and adding one is a change to
  /// this enum and a `match` arm that the checker will not let anybody forget.
  export enum Program
    case RevenueSummary
    case ConfirmedBookings
    case RateCard
    /// The columns this transformation's output carries, in order.
    export fn columns(self) -> Array<String>
    /// The name `--program` selects this transformation with.
    export fn name(self) -> String
    /// The format this transformation reads.
    export fn reads(self) -> Format
    /// What this transformation does, in one line, for `--help`.
    export fn summary(self) -> String
    /// The format this transformation writes when nothing says otherwise.
    ///
    /// A default rather than a requirement: every transformation's output is a
    /// row of cells, and a cell renders in either format, so `--output-format`
    /// may always override this.
    export fn writes(self) -> Format
  /// What the rate-card transformation carries between records.
  ///
  /// Only whether the header has gone past. A CSV file names its columns on its
  /// first line, and a reader that is handed one line at a time has to remember
  /// that it has seen it.
  export struct RateCard
    field seenHeader: Bool
    field rows: Int
  /// What a revenue summary accumulates.
  ///
  /// One entry per property, and nothing else: the bookings themselves are read,
  /// counted, and dropped, so what this holds is bounded by how many properties
  /// the input mentions rather than by how long the input is.
  export struct Revenue
    field properties: Map<String, Totals>
  /// The empty state a run starts from.
  export fn emptyConfirmed() -> NoState
  /// The empty state a run starts from.
  export fn emptyRateCard() -> RateCard
  /// The empty summary a run starts from.
  export fn emptyRevenue() -> Revenue
  /// Writes nothing at the end, because everything was written on the way
  /// through.
  export fn finishConfirmed(state: NoState) -> Array<Array<Cell>>
  /// Writes nothing at the end: every row went out as it was read.
  export fn finishRateCard(state: RateCard) -> Array<Array<Cell>>
  /// Writes one row per property, in ascending order by name.
  ///
  /// The order is the `Map`'s own, which is ascending by key, so two runs over
  /// the same input produce the same file and a golden test is possible.
  export fn finishRevenue(state: Revenue) -> Array<Array<Cell>>
  /// Keeps one record when it is confirmed, and writes it out at once.
  export fn foldConfirmed(state: NoState, line: String, number: Int) -> Result<Step<NoState>, Detail>
  /// Reads one CSV line, checking the header and normalizing every row after
  /// it.
  export fn foldRateCard(state: RateCard, line: String, number: Int) -> Result<Step<RateCard>, Detail>
  /// Folds one JSON Lines record into the summary.
  ///
  /// A cancelled booking is read and then ignored. It is not an error -- a
  /// cancellation is an ordinary thing for a booking to be -- and it is not
  /// revenue either, so the count it does not join is the count of bookings that
  /// earned something.
  export fn foldRevenue(state: Revenue, line: String, number: Int) -> Result<Step<Revenue>, Detail>
  /// Reads a transformation by name, or reports the ones there are.
  export fn programNamed(name: String) -> Result<Program, Error>
  /// Every transformation this package declares, in the order `--help` lists
  /// them.
  export fn programs() -> Array<Program>

module cq.records
  /// A booking, as this program requires one to be.
  ///
  /// Every field is required and every field has a type. That is the point of
  /// the type: past this struct nothing in the program has to ask whether
  /// `nights` was a number, and nothing has to decide what to do when it was
  /// not. The decision is made once, here, where the record is still next to the
  /// line it came from.
  export struct Booking
    field id: String
    field guest: String
    field property: String
    field checkIn: String
    field nights: Int
    field guests: Int
    field rate: Float
    field status: Status
    field channel: String
    /// What this booking is worth, which is its nightly rate for every night of
    /// it.
    export fn revenue(self) -> Float
  /// What a booking's `status` field may say.
  ///
  /// An unrecognized status is an error rather than a case, because a status
  /// this program has never heard of is a fact about the input that the program
  /// should report rather than average.
  export enum Status
    case Confirmed
    case Pending
    case Cancelled
    /// The word this status is written with, which is the word it was read
    /// from.
    export fn name(self) -> String
  /// Reads a booking out of one parsed record.
  ///
  /// The column is 1 for every failure here, and that is a limitation rather
  /// than a choice: a `Json` value has forgotten where in the line it was
  /// written, so the most this can say is which record was wrong and which field
  /// of it. Carrying a span on every value is what a diagnostic layer would do,
  /// and this program does not have one.
  export fn bookingFrom(record: Json) -> Result<Booking, Detail>

module cq.rows
  /// One value in an output row.
  ///
  /// A row is not an array of strings, because the two formats this program
  /// writes disagree about what a string is: CSV has only text, and JSON Lines
  /// distinguishes `3` from `"3"`. Deciding that once per value, here, is what
  /// lets one program's output go out in either format without the program
  /// knowing which.
  export enum Cell
    case Text(String)
    case Count(Int)
    case Decimal(Float, Int)
  /// A format this program writes.
  export enum Format
    case Jsonl
    case Csv
    /// The name the command line selects this format with.
    export fn name(self) -> String
  /// What one record produced: the state it left behind, and the rows to write
  /// for it now.
  ///
  /// This is the one shape every transformation's step answers in, and it is
  /// what lets an aggregation and a filter be the same kind of thing. An
  /// aggregation returns no rows until its input runs out and everything it
  /// knows is in the state; a filter returns a row per record it keeps and
  /// carries almost nothing. The engine writes whatever comes back at once, so a
  /// filter over a hundred thousand records never holds more than one row.
  export struct Step<S>
    field state: S
    field rows: Array<Array<Cell>>
  /// Reads a format by name, or reports the two there are.
  export fn formatNamed(name: String) -> Result<Format, Error>
  /// The header line `format` starts a file with, if it has one.
  ///
  /// JSON Lines has no header: every record carries its own field names, so a
  /// first line naming them would be a record that is not one.
  export fn header(format: Format, columns: Array<String>) -> Option<String>
  /// Renders one row in `format`, under the column names `columns`.
  ///
  /// CSV names its columns once, in a header the caller writes; JSON Lines names
  /// them on every record, which is why the column names are needed here and not
  /// only there.
  export fn renderRow(format: Format, columns: Array<String>, cells: Array<Cell>) -> String

module hello
  /// Returns a greeting for `name`.
  export fn greeting(name: String) -> String
  /// Runs the command-line program.
  export fn main(args: Array<String>) -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires console

module httpstatus
  /// HTTP status codes this package recognizes, derived from
  /// `files/status_codes.txt` by `codegen.statusCodes`.
  export enum StatusCode
    case Ok
    case Created
    case NoContent
    case BadRequest
    case Unauthorized
    case Forbidden
    case NotFound
    case Conflict
    case UnprocessableEntity
    case InternalServerError
    case ServiceUnavailable
    /// The numeric HTTP status code.
    export fn code(self) -> Int

module restricted
  /// Reads only through the document capability supplied by the host.
  ///
  /// `console` is reached only through `text.report`, so this module requires
  /// the console capability without naming a host module for it.
  export fn main() -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires console, documents

module rules
  /// Decides one of the samples, named by its position, and makes no Host API
  /// call at all.
  ///
  /// A control rather than a feature. `rules.embedded.decideRequest` fetches its
  /// pull request through the Host API and reports the decision back through it;
  /// this reaches the same `decide` over a pull request the package already
  /// holds. The difference between the two, invoked the same number of times on
  /// the same machine, is what the boundary costs, and
  /// `examples/rules/README.md` is where that number is.
  ///
  /// It takes its argument as text for the same reason `decideRequest` does:
  /// an entry may take one `Array<String>` and nothing else.
  export fn decideSample(args: Array<String>) -> Result<Decision, Error>
    capability-open
  /// Answers immediately, having done nothing.
  ///
  /// The other control: what one invocation costs before the program it invokes
  /// does anything. Finding the entry, building the `Array<String>` of
  /// arguments, entering the frame, and answering is all this measures, and
  /// every other number in the README stands on top of it.
  export fn floor(args: Array<String>) -> Result<Int, Error>
  /// Prints the catalog, and then what it decides about every sample.
  ///
  /// This entry exists so that the rule package is a program somebody can run
  /// and read the output of, and so that it joins the differential corpus that
  /// runs every `[run.<name>]` on both backends and compares the answers. The
  /// embedding this example is really about does not call `main` at all: it
  /// calls `rules.embedded.decideRequest`, one pull request at a time, from
  /// Rust. See `examples/rules/README.md`.
  export fn main() -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires console
    capability-open

module rules.catalog
  /// Asks which branch the change is aimed at.
  export struct BranchRule
    field protected: String
    field reviewers: Int
    conforms rules.catalog.Rule
    /// What this rule found in `pr`, or `None` when it found nothing.
    export fn appraise(self, pr: PullRequest) -> Option<Finding>
    /// One line saying what this rule is looking for.
    ///
    /// Defaulted, because a rule whose name says it all should not have to
    /// write this out, and because a default body is the thing this example is
    /// here to exercise: `describes` is dispatched dynamically like the other
    /// two and is implemented by only three of the six rules below.
    export fn describes(self) -> String
    /// The name this rule is recorded under, which is what a finding carries
    /// back to whoever has to act on it.
    export fn name(self) -> String
  /// Asks whether the change is still a draft.
  export struct DraftRule
    conforms rules.catalog.Rule
    /// What this rule found in `pr`, or `None` when it found nothing.
    export fn appraise(self, pr: PullRequest) -> Option<Finding>
    /// One line saying what this rule is looking for.
    ///
    /// Defaulted, because a rule whose name says it all should not have to
    /// write this out, and because a default body is the thing this example is
    /// here to exercise: `describes` is dispatched dynamically like the other
    /// two and is implemented by only three of the six rules below.
    export fn describes(self) -> String
    /// The name this rule is recorded under, which is what a finding carries
    /// back to whoever has to act on it.
    export fn name(self) -> String
  /// Asks whether the change reaches a directory the repository guards.
  ///
  /// The guarded prefixes are a `Set` and not an `Array` because the question
  /// asked of them is membership by prefix rather than order, and because the
  /// set is written once and read for every pull request afterwards.
  export struct GuardedPathRule
    field prefixes: Set<String>
    field waiver: String
    conforms rules.catalog.Rule
    /// What this rule found in `pr`, or `None` when it found nothing.
    export fn appraise(self, pr: PullRequest) -> Option<Finding>
    /// One line saying what this rule is looking for.
    ///
    /// Defaulted, because a rule whose name says it all should not have to
    /// write this out, and because a default body is the thing this example is
    /// here to exercise: `describes` is dispatched dynamically like the other
    /// two and is implemented by only three of the six rules below.
    export fn describes(self) -> String
    /// The name this rule is recorded under, which is what a finding carries
    /// back to whoever has to act on it.
    export fn name(self) -> String
  /// Asks what the labels on the change are worth.
  ///
  /// A `Map` from label to the reviewers that label costs. The heaviest label a
  /// pull request carries is the one that answers; they do not add, for the
  /// reason `Severity` gives.
  export struct LabelRule
    field weights: Map<String, Int>
    conforms rules.catalog.Rule
    /// What this rule found in `pr`, or `None` when it found nothing.
    export fn appraise(self, pr: PullRequest) -> Option<Finding>
    /// One line saying what this rule is looking for.
    ///
    /// Defaulted, because a rule whose name says it all should not have to
    /// write this out, and because a default body is the thing this example is
    /// here to exercise: `describes` is dispatched dynamically like the other
    /// two and is implemented by only three of the six rules below.
    export fn describes(self) -> String
    /// The name this rule is recorded under, which is what a finding carries
    /// back to whoever has to act on it.
    export fn name(self) -> String
  /// One question a review policy asks about one pull request.
  ///
  /// A rule answers `None` when it has nothing to say, which is the ordinary
  /// case: most rules are silent about most pull requests, and a rule that had
  /// to answer with a "nothing found" finding would make the engine filter what
  /// it should never have been handed.
  export trait Rule
    fn name(self) -> String
    fn appraise(self, pr: PullRequest) -> Option<Finding>
    fn describes(self) -> String (default)
  /// Asks how large the change is.
  export struct SizeRule
    field threshold: Int
    field reviewers: Int
    conforms rules.catalog.Rule
    /// What this rule found in `pr`, or `None` when it found nothing.
    export fn appraise(self, pr: PullRequest) -> Option<Finding>
    /// One line saying what this rule is looking for.
    ///
    /// Defaulted, because a rule whose name says it all should not have to
    /// write this out, and because a default body is the thing this example is
    /// here to exercise: `describes` is dispatched dynamically like the other
    /// two and is implemented by only three of the six rules below.
    export fn describes(self) -> String
    /// The name this rule is recorded under, which is what a finding carries
    /// back to whoever has to act on it.
    export fn name(self) -> String
  /// Asks whether a change of any size arrived without tests.
  export struct TestedRule
    field floor: Int
    conforms rules.catalog.Rule
    /// What this rule found in `pr`, or `None` when it found nothing.
    export fn appraise(self, pr: PullRequest) -> Option<Finding>
    /// One line saying what this rule is looking for.
    ///
    /// Defaulted, because a rule whose name says it all should not have to
    /// write this out, and because a default body is the thing this example is
    /// here to exercise: `describes` is dispatched dynamically like the other
    /// two and is implemented by only three of the six rules below.
    export fn describes(self) -> String
    /// The name this rule is recorded under, which is what a finding carries
    /// back to whoever has to act on it.
    export fn name(self) -> String
  /// Asks one rule about one pull request without dispatching dynamically.
  ///
  /// `rules.engine.appraise` walks an `Array<dyn Rule>` and therefore dispatches
  /// through a `dyn`; this is the same call written against a bounded type
  /// parameter, so the two dispatch forms stand side by side in one package.
  /// The tests below call both and assert they answer the same thing.
  export fn ask<R: Rule>(rule: R, pr: PullRequest) -> Option<Finding>
    capability-open
  /// The catalog this package ships, in the order its findings are weighed.
  ///
  /// The array is written out here rather than assembled from configuration
  /// because a rule is code: every one of the six is a type with a body, the
  /// checker knows all six implement `Rule`, and the only thing chosen at run
  /// time is which of them had something to say. An engine that loaded rules
  /// from a file would have to decide what to do about a rule it could not
  /// understand, and this one never has to.
  export fn standard() -> Array<dyn Rule>

module rules.embedded
  /// Decides the one pull request the host names, and reports the decision back
  /// to it.
  ///
  /// This is the function the Rust host in `examples/rules/host/` invokes, once
  /// per application request, against a module it compiled and lowered once.
  /// Everything about it is shaped by what an embedding can and cannot do
  /// today, and each of those is worth stating rather than leaving to be
  /// inferred from the code.
  ///
  /// The request identifier arrives as a process argument, because
  /// `Vm::run_entry` and `Interpreter::run_entry` take `Vec<Rc<str>>` and
  /// nothing else: there is no public way to call an exported Cove function
  /// with a Rust-built argument, which is issue #150. So the pull request
  /// itself cannot be passed in, and comes back through `reviews.pull` instead
  /// -- which is the Host API boundary, and is therefore also the thing whose
  /// cost the embedding measures.
  ///
  /// The decision leaves by both routes at once, on purpose. It is returned, so
  /// the host reads a typed `rules.policy.Decision` out of the run's answer, and
  /// it is also handed to `reviews.record`, so the same decision crosses the
  /// boundary in the other direction under the request identifier that started
  /// it. The two are what a trace links: every `HostCall` event this run writes
  /// carries the identifier, because both calls were given it.
  export fn decideRequest(args: Array<String>) -> Result<Decision, Error>
    requires reviews
    capability-open
  /// Fetches the pull request the host holds under `requestId`, and answers
  /// nothing else.
  ///
  /// The embedding invokes this on its own as the control that separates what
  /// the boundary costs from what the rules cost: it makes the same inbound
  /// call and the same conversion as `decideRequest` and then weighs nothing.
  export fn pullOnly(args: Array<String>) -> Result<PullRequest, Error>
    requires reviews

module rules.engine
  /// The decision `catalog` reaches about `pr`.
  ///
  /// Split from `decide` so that a test can ask one rule, or three, without
  /// having to arrange a pull request that the other five stay quiet about.
  export fn appraise(pr: PullRequest, catalog: Array<dyn Rule>) -> Decision
    capability-open
  /// The decision the shipped catalog reaches about `pr`.
  ///
  /// This is the one function an embedding calls. It takes a pull request and
  /// answers a decision, and everything between the two is this package's
  /// business: which rules exist, in what order they are weighed, and how their
  /// findings become one policy.
  export fn decide(pr: PullRequest) -> Decision
    capability-open
  /// Every finding the catalog has about `pr`, most serious first.
  ///
  /// `sorted(by:)` is stable, so rules that answered at the same severity keep
  /// the order the catalog put them in. That is what makes the trail a decision
  /// prints reproducible: the catalog is written down, so the order is too.
  export fn findings(pr: PullRequest, catalog: Array<dyn Rule>) -> Array<Finding>
    capability-open
  /// The one policy `found` argues for.
  ///
  /// Three cases and they are tried in this order for a reason. A blocking
  /// finding decides on its own, whatever else was found, because a block is
  /// not a quantity that other findings can outweigh. Otherwise the reviewers
  /// asked for are the most any one finding asked for, and the reason is that
  /// finding's, because a reason assembled out of six of them is a sentence
  /// nobody reads.
  export fn policyFor(found: Array<Finding>) -> ReviewPolicy

module rules.fixtures
  /// A small change with tests, on an ordinary branch: nothing to say.
  export fn clean() -> PullRequest
  /// A draft nobody has asked for review on yet: advisory only.
  export fn draft() -> PullRequest
  /// A change that reaches a guarded directory without a waiver: blocked.
  export fn guarded() -> PullRequest
  /// A change aimed at the protected branch, carrying the heaviest label.
  export fn labelled() -> PullRequest
  /// A change over the size threshold, with tests: reviewers, and why.
  export fn large() -> PullRequest
  /// The sample at `at`, counting from zero, or `None` when there is none.
  ///
  /// Written as a chain of comparisons rather than as `samples().get(at)`,
  /// and the reason is the measurement in `examples/rules/host/`. The control
  /// it runs against the embedded entry has to build exactly one pull request,
  /// because the invocation it is a control on receives exactly one; going
  /// through `samples()` would build all six and charge the control for five
  /// pull requests the host never sent.
  export fn sample(at: Int) -> Option<PullRequest>
  /// The pull requests this package is demonstrated and tested on.
  ///
  /// Written down in Cove rather than read from a file, and the reason is the
  /// embedding this example exists for: `examples/rules/host/` builds the same
  /// six records in Rust and hands them across the Host API boundary, and the
  /// test that pins the two paths against each other needs one of them to be
  /// somewhere a Cove test can reach. A JSON file would have put a parser
  /// between the fixture and the assertion, and this package has no opinion
  /// about JSON.
  ///
  /// Each of the six reaches a different arm of the policy, which is what makes
  /// `rules.main`'s output worth reading rather than six copies of `normal`.
  export fn samples() -> Array<PullRequest>
  /// The same guarded directory, with the waiver label: reviewers instead.
  export fn waived() -> PullRequest

module rules.policy
  /// A policy, and every finding that argued for it.
  ///
  /// The findings ride along because a decision nobody can account for is one
  /// nobody can argue with. `ReviewPolicy` is what a caller acts on; the
  /// findings are what it shows the author.
  export struct Decision
    field policy: ReviewPolicy
    field findings: Array<Finding>
    /// This decision as one line, for a console or a log.
    export fn line(self) -> String
    /// The rules that argued for this decision, in the order they were weighed,
    /// as one comma-separated list.
    export fn trail(self) -> String
  /// One thing a rule noticed about one pull request.
  ///
  /// A finding names the rule that made it, so a decision can be read back to
  /// the rule that caused it without the engine keeping a second table of which
  /// answer came from where.
  export struct Finding
    field rule: String
    field severity: Severity
    field reason: String
    field reviewers: Int
  /// A pull request, as a review policy requires one to be.
  ///
  /// Ten fields and not one of them optional. The engine never asks whether a
  /// field was supplied, which is the point of writing the type down: whoever
  /// hands a pull request in decides once, at the boundary, what to do about a
  /// record that is missing something. Past this struct there is no such
  /// record.
  export struct PullRequest
    field id: String
    field title: String
    field author: String
    field targetBranch: String
    field changedLines: Int
    field filesTouched: Array<String>
    field labels: Array<String>
    field approvals: Int
    field isDraft: Bool
    field hasTests: Bool
    /// The labels as a set, which is what a membership question wants.
    ///
    /// The field itself stays an `Array`, because that is the shape a host can
    /// hand one over in -- a Host API schema has no `Set`, which is issue #153
    /// -- and the conversion lives here rather than at the boundary so that the
    /// embedded caller and the fixtures below reach it by the same route.
    export fn labelSet(self) -> Set<String>
    /// Whether this pull request carries `label`.
    export fn labelled(self, label: String) -> Bool
    /// Whether any file this pull request touches sits under `prefix`.
    export fn touches(self, prefix: String) -> Bool
  /// What a `ReviewPolicy.Require` asks for.
  ///
  /// A struct rather than two positional payload values, because an enum case's
  /// payload is positional in Cove and `Require(2, "large_change")` says less at
  /// the call site than the two labels do.
  export struct Requirement
    field reviewers: Int
    field reason: String
  /// What a review policy demands of one pull request.
  export enum ReviewPolicy
    case Normal
    case Require(Requirement)
    case Block(String)
    /// This policy's name, which is the word a host records.
    export fn name(self) -> String
    /// Why this policy was reached, in the words a decision record carries.
    export fn reason(self) -> String
    /// How many reviewers this policy asks for, which is none unless it is
    /// asking for reviewers.
    export fn reviewers(self) -> Int
  /// How much attention one finding asks for.
  ///
  /// Three named levels rather than a number, because what the engine answers
  /// with is a decision about kind and not about degree. Two advisory findings
  /// do not add up to a required one, and no quantity of required ones becomes
  /// a block; a number would invite exactly that arithmetic and then have to
  /// document that it means nothing.
  export enum Severity
    case Advisory
    case Required
    case Blocking
    /// This level's name, as a decision record spells it.
    export fn name(self) -> String
    /// Where this level sits against the other two, ascending.
    ///
    /// Ordering is the whole of what this means. Nothing sums these.
    export fn rank(self) -> Int
    /// Whether a finding at this level stops the change.
    export fn stops(self) -> Bool

module server
  /// JSON body returned by the health endpoint.
  export struct HealthResponse
    field status: String
  /// Returns a stable health response without external I/O.
  export fn health(request: http.Request) -> http.Response
    requires http
  /// Runs the HTTP server.
  ///
  /// The loop belongs to the program rather than to the host: `handle` answers
  /// one request and returns, so the run's fuel, deadline, and cancellation
  /// reach a server exactly as they reach any other Cove code. It ends when the
  /// listener has nothing more to serve.
  export fn main() -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires console, http

module tasks
  /// Data needed to render the dashboard.
  export struct Dashboard
    field bookings: String
    field prices: String
  /// Loads independent dashboard inputs concurrently.
  ///
  /// The two fetches run on threads of their own, and `clock.timeout` bounds the
  /// wait for both together: a body it stops does not finish, and the error
  /// names the bound rather than whatever the stopped body was doing.
  export async fn loadDashboard() -> Result<Dashboard, Error>
    requires clock, http

module text
  /// Reports the word count of `text` on the console the host granted.
  export fn report(text: String) -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires console
  /// Counts words in `text`.
  export fn wordCount(text: String) -> Int

module traits
  /// A room booking.
  export struct Booking
    field id: Int
    field guests: Int
    conforms traits.Summary
    /// Returns the line this value takes in a report, which defaults to its
    /// summary as an ordinary bullet.
    export fn line(self) -> String
    /// Returns the one-line summary of this value.
    export fn summarize(self) -> String
  /// A payment recorded against a booking.
  export struct Receipt
    field bookingId: Int
    field cents: Int
    conforms traits.Summary
    /// Returns the line this value takes in a report, which defaults to its
    /// summary as an ordinary bullet.
    export fn line(self) -> String
    /// Returns the one-line summary of this value.
    export fn summarize(self) -> String
  /// A value that can summarise itself for a human-readable report.
  export trait Summary
    fn summarize(self) -> String
    fn line(self) -> String (default)
  /// Headlines one entry.
  ///
  /// The bound is checked at the call site, which is also where `T` is chosen,
  /// so `summarize` resolves to exactly one implementation. That is why this
  /// function takes one entry rather than a mixed collection: every value it
  /// sees has the same type.
  export fn headline<T: Summary>(entry: T) -> String
    capability-open
  /// Prints a report built both ways.
  export fn main() -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires console
    capability-open
  /// Renders a report of entries whose types may differ.
  ///
  /// `dyn Summary` values carry their implementation, so `line` is resolved
  /// from each value rather than from the signature. That is what lets one
  /// array hold a `Booking` and a `Receipt` at once.
  export fn report(entries: Array<dyn Summary>) -> String
    capability-open

module values
  /// Completed immutable booking data.
  export struct Booking
    field status: BookingStatus
    field guests: Array<String>
  /// A value whose scalar field copies and whose Vector field shares storage.
  export struct BookingDraft
    field status: BookingStatus
    field guests: Vector<String>
  /// Lifecycle state of a booking.
  export enum BookingStatus
    case Pending
    case Confirmed
  /// Exercises Cove's value copies, Vector aliases, and freeze transition.
  export fn main() -> Result<Unit, Error>
    requires console
